following three conditions are equivalent:

1. $x$ is stationary for the action $S$ of $L$;
2. $E_{L}(x)(t)=0$ for every $t\in[a,b]$;
3. $\mathsf M x''(t)=-\nabla_{x}U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)$ for every $t\in[a,b]$.

Condition 3 is the model's equation of motion of the potential branch
([[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv)) written along the curve for the
presentation $(U,d)$ with the potential part alone: the residual forces $d$ do
not appear, and the statement is therefore a statement about the potential
part of the force map. No existence of curves satisfying these conditions is
asserted.

Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] and let $q:[a,b]\to U$ be a $C^2$ admissible curve.
Then $q$ is stationary for the action $S$ if and only if

$$E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t)=0\qquad\text{for every }t\in[a,b].$$

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$ and $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]).
Assume the presentation has **no residual forces**, $d\equiv0$, so that the
force map itself is $F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)$. Then:

1. **motions are stationary.** If $x:J\to Q$ is a motion of the model on an
   interval $J$ with nonempty interior ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) and
   $a<b$ with $[a,b]\subseteq J\cap I_{0}$, then the restriction $x|_{[a,b]}$
   is stationary for the action $S$ on $[a,b]$.

2. **stationary curves are restrictions of motions.** If $a<b$ with
   $[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$ and $x:[a,b]\to Q$ is a $C^{2}$ admissible curve that
   is stationary for $S$, then $x$ is the restriction to $[a,b]$ of the
   maximal motion of the model through the initial datum
   $\bigl(a,x(a),x'(a)\bigr)$ (whose existence and uniqueness are
   [[pthm-cm02-ivp]] clause 4); in particular the maximal interval of that
   motion contains $[a,b]$.

3. **identification.** Consequently the $C^{2}$ curves $x:[a,b]\to Q$ that are
   stationary for the action are exactly the restrictions to $[a,b]$ of the
   motions of the model whose maximal interval contains $[a,b]$, and the model
   equation satisfied is $\mathsf M x''=-\nabla_{x}U$ on that interval.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and on the declared
potential presentation with $d\equiv0$; it asserts no existence of stationary
curves for arbitrary endpoint data, no minimisation and no empirical value.

Let $\mathcal L:J\times U\times\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be a fibre-full $C^2$ time-dependent
Lagrangian chart that is hyperregular, with inverse Legendre branch $v(t,q,p)$ and Hamiltonian
$H(t,q,p)=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\mathcal L(t,q,v(t,q,p))$
([[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]). Then:

1. **(differential)** for every $(t,q,p)\in J\times U\times\mathbb R^n$,

$$H_p(t,q,p)=v(t,q,p),\qquad H_q(t,q,p)=-\mathcal L_q\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr),\qquad H_t(t,q,p)=-\mathcal L_t\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr);$$

2. **(equivalence)** for a $C^1$ curve $(q,p):I\to U\times\mathbb R^n$ on an open interval $I\subseteq J$
   ([[def-interval]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]) the following are
   equivalent:
   (a) $q$ is $C^2$ and $E_{\mathcal L}(q)(t)=0$ for all $t\in I$, with
   $p(t)=\mathcal L_v\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)$;
   (b) $(q,p)$ satisfies Hamilton's equations
   $q'(t)=H_p\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)$ and $p'(t)=-H_q\bigl(t,q(t),p(t)\bigr)$ for all $t\in I$;
3. **(energy)** along any curve satisfying (a) or (b), the function
   $e(t):=\mathcal L_v(t,q,q')\cdot q'(t)-\mathcal L(t,q(t),q'(t))$ equals $H(t,q(t),p(t))$ and
   satisfies $e'(t)=-\mathcal L_t(t,q(t),q'(t))$ on $I$; in particular, if $\mathcal L_t$ vanishes
   on the set $\{(s,q(s),q'(s)):s\in I\}$, then $e$ is constant on $I$.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$,
kinetic metric $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$ and substituted
potential $\widetilde U(t,q)=U(t,X(q))$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]), and let $H$ and
$\widetilde H$ be the Hamiltonians of [[def-cm12-hamiltonian]]. Then:

1. **(Cartesian chart)** The fibre momentum map
   $\mathbb F_{t,x}(v)=\mathsf Mv$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ onto
   $\mathbb R^{3N}$ for every $(t,x)\in I_{0}\times Q$, and the inverse
   Legendre branch is the $C^{2}$ map
   $v(t,x,p)=\mathsf M^{-1}p$ on the whole phase chart
   $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the Cartesian chart in the sense of
   [[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], and the Hamiltonian of the branch is

$$H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x),$$

with the dot product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

2. **(generalized-coordinate chart)** The fibre map
   $v\mapsto G(q)v$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^{r}$ onto $\mathbb R^{r}$
   for every $(t,q)\in I_{0}\times\Omega$, and the inverse Legendre branch is
   the $C^{2}$ map $v(t,q,p)=G(q)^{-1}p$ on
   $I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$. Hence the presentation is
   hyperregular on the chart of $X$, and the Hamiltonian in the coordinates
   $X$ is

$$\widetilde H(t,q,p)=\tfrac12\,p\cdot G(q)^{-1}p+\widetilde U(t,q),$$

   a $C^{2}$ function of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.

The statement is conditional on the adopted force branch and the declared
presentation; it asserts no equation of motion, no conservation law and no
empirical content.

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] with the
data and conventions of [[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]: masses
$m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U$ and residual forces $d$ of
the standing regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]); dimensions are read by
[[def-cm01-units]] and the Euclidean pairing is
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

**(a) Cartesian Hamiltonian.** Assume the presentation is hyperregular on the
Cartesian chart, with inverse Legendre branch
$v:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]], [[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]]).
The **Hamiltonian of the presentation on the Cartesian chart** is the function

$$H:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad H(t,x,p):=p\cdot v(t,x,p)-L\bigl(t,x,v(t,x,p)\bigr),$$

where $p\cdot v(t,x,p)$ is the Euclidean pairing of the momentum covector
with the inverse-branch velocity ([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). The momentum phase chart
$I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with coordinates $(t,x,p)$ is the
**Hamiltonian phase chart** of the presentation on the Cartesian chart.
If $Q=\varnothing$, the formula denotes the unique empty function; the
identification with the cited mathematical fibre-full chart applies only
when $Q\ne\varnothing$.

**(b) Generalized-coordinate Hamiltonian.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a
generalized-coordinate map with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, kinetic
metric $G$ and inverse Legendre branch $v$ on
$I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}$ ([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]],
[[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]). The **Hamiltonian of the presentation in the
coordinates $X$** is

$$\widetilde H:I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad \widetilde H(t,q,p):=p\cdot v(t,q,p)-\widetilde L\bigl(t,q,v(t,q,p)\bigr).$$

For the Cartesian chart when $Q\ne\varnothing$, $X=\mathrm{id}$ and
$\widetilde H=H$; the general
definition is the same formula applied to the substituted fibre-full chart.

**(c) Dimensions and conventions.** Each term of the defining difference has
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy): the pairing $p\cdot v$ multiplies
$\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ by $\ell\tau^{-1}$ in Cartesian data
([[def-cm12-cotangent-momentum]]), and $L$ has energy dimension
([[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]). In the coordinates $X$ the
pairing is dimensionally consistent for every declared coordinate dimension
$\gamma_{a}$ and the dimension is unchanged. The Hamiltonian is $C^{1}$ on
its domain, being a sum of products of $C^{1}$ maps
([[thm-ck-euclidean-maps-closed-under-algebra-and-composition]],
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). The pairing is the coordinate
Euclidean product; no metric on momentum space and no symplectic form is
introduced by this definition.

**(d) Dependence and status.** The Hamiltonian depends on the declared chart,
on its inverse Legendre branch, uniquely determined on that chart by fibre
bijectivity ([[def-cm12-hyperregularity]]), and on the potential
representative: replacing $U$ by $U+c(t)$ leaves the branch unchanged and
replaces $L$ by $L-c(t)$, hence replaces $H$ by $H+c(t)$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c),
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] clause (b)). It asserts no
equation of motion, no conservation property and no measured value; the
explicit kinetic-plus-potential form of $H$ for the mechanical branch, the
equivalence of its equations with the model's equation of motion and its
relation to the mechanical energy are the theorems of this page. Matrix
identities used by those theorems are read through
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], in the
fixed inertial frame with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ used there: $N\ge1$
labels with masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), $C^{2}$ potential $U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d$ of the standing
regularity ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]],
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]]). Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]],
the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
and gradients and Jacobians are those of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]
and [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

**(a) Cartesian momentum.** For a state $(t,x,v)\in I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
define the **momentum of the labels** by

$$p(t,x,v):=\mathsf M v\;=\;(m_{1}v_{1},\dots,m_{N}v_{N}),$$

whose label components are $p_{i}=m_{i}v_{i}$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]
clause (d)); its dimension is $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$). The space $\mathbb R^{3N}$ is
identified with its dual by the Euclidean inner product, so that $p$ is a
**covector** acting on a velocity $w$ by the dot product $p\cdot w$. The pair
$(x,p)$ is the **cotangent datum** of the state, and $I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
with coordinates $(t,x,p)$ is the **momentum phase chart** of the
presentation.

**(b) Fibre derivative.** The **fibre derivative** of the presentation is
the velocity-slot gradient $p:=L_{v}(t,x,v)$ at each state. When
$Q\ne\varnothing$, this is the momentum coordinate of the Legendre
map of the fibre-full chart $(O,L)$ of clause (c) of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], in the sense of
[[def-cm-legendre-map-in-a-time-dependent-chart]] (the chart data are those of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Because $L=K-U$ with
$K'(v)=\mathsf Mv$ and $U$ independent of the velocity slot (clause (a) of
[[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]]), one has
$L_{v}(t,x,v)=\mathsf Mv$: the fibre derivative and the momentum of
clause (a) are the same covector, and for $Q\ne\varnothing$ the Legendre map
of the presentation is $(t,x,v)\mapsto(t,x,\mathsf Mv)$. If
$Q=\varnothing$, the state and momentum domains are empty and the momentum
and fibre-derivative assignments are the unique empty maps; there is no
fibre-full chart instance of the cited mathematical definition.

**(c) Generalized momenta.** Let $X:\Omega\to Q$ be a generalized-coordinate
map of the model, with substituted Lagrangian $\widetilde L$, substituted
potential $\widetilde U$ and kinetic metric $G(q)=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q)$
([[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]] clauses (a)-(b),
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]]).
The **generalized momentum** of the presentation in the coordinates $X$ is
the covector

$$p(t,q,v):=\widetilde L_{v}(t,q,v)=G(q)v,$$

whose components $p_{a}=\partial\widetilde L/\partial v_{a}$ have dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}\gamma_{a}^{-1}$ (action divided by the dimension
$\gamma_{a}$ of the coordinate $q_{a}$), while the **pairing**
$p\cdot v=\sum_{a}p_{a}v^{a}$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For the
Cartesian chart when $Q\ne\varnothing$, $X=\mathrm{id}$, $\Omega=Q$,
$G=\mathsf M$, and clause (c) reduces to clause (a). If $Q=\varnothing$,
no generalized-coordinate map exists, since its domain $\Omega$ is nonempty.

**(d) Status and warnings.** The item defines the momentum datum of a declared
presentation as a model object. It introduces no force law, no equation of
motion and no measured value; it depends on the declared chart and on the
declared coordinate dimensions $\gamma_{a}$, and it is independent of the
residual forces $d$ and of the normalization $U\mapsto U+c(t)$ of the
potential representative ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]
clause (c)). The momentum is not in general mass times coordinate velocity: in
the coordinates $X$ it is $G(q)v$, and the identity $p_{i}=m_{i}v_{i}$ is
specific to Cartesian data. The evaluation of the velocity Hessian, the
invertibility of the fiberwise momentum map, the Hamiltonian of an inverse
branch and the evolution equations are the subject of the other items of this
page, not of this definition. All differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

Adopt the force model with potential presentation $(U,d)$ and mechanical
Lagrangian $L=K-U$ of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]], with
masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$,
time window $I_{0}$, mass operator $\mathsf M$ and $C^{2}$ potential
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ ([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]).
Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]]; gradients and Jacobians are those of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], transposes those of
[[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]], and $C^{r}$ classes those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].

**(a) Generalized-coordinate map.** Let $r\ge1$ and let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{r}$ be open and nonempty. A **generalized-coordinate
map of the model** is a map $X:\Omega\to Q$ of class $C^{3}$ whose derivative
$DX(q)$ is injective for every $q\in\Omega$
([[def-euclidean-submersions-and-immersions]]: an immersion); the coordinates
$q=(q_{1},\dots,q_{r})$ each carry a declared dimension $\gamma_{i}$ and unit
fixed as part of the model declaration. When $r=3N$, injectivity makes
$DX(q):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ a bijection: its kernel is $\{0\}$,
so rank-nullity gives image dimension $3N$, equal to the target dimension.
The inverse is linear: if $y_{1}=DX(q)u_{1}$ and $y_{2}=DX(q)u_{2}$, then
linearity and uniqueness of preimages give
$DX(q)^{-1}(a y_{1}+b y_{2})=a u_{1}+b u_{2}$. Thus $DX(q)$ is invertible in
the sense of [[def-invertible-euclidean-linear-map]]. The inverse-function
theorem and its higher-regularity result
([[thm-euclidean-inverse-function-theorem]],
[[thm-higher-regularity-of-local-inverses]]) make $X$ a local $C^{3}$
diffeomorphism at each point. This local property does not imply that $X$ is
globally one-to-one: call $X$ a global coordinate chart onto $X(\Omega)$ only
when it is also injective. The other intended case is $r=3N-k$ for an integer
$k$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, where $X$ may be a surjective immersion of a regular
holonomic-constraint locus as in clause (d); injectivity is not required there.
The **admissible coordinate curves** are the $C^{2}$ maps $q:J\to\Omega$ on an
interval $J\subseteq I_{0}$ with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]); each such
curve induces the configuration curve $x:=X\circ q:J\to Q$.

**(b) Substituted Lagrangian and kinetic metric.** For a generalized-coordinate
map $X$ define

$$\widetilde L:I_{0}\times\Omega\times\mathbb R^{r}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad \widetilde L(t,q,v):=L\bigl(t,X(q),DX(q)v\bigr)=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}G(q)v-\widetilde U(t,q),$$

with the **kinetic metric** and the substituted potential

$$G(q):=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q),\qquad \widetilde U(t,q):=U\bigl(t,X(q)\bigr).$$

$G(q)$ is symmetric and positive definite, because $DX(q)$ is injective and
$\mathsf M$ is symmetric positive definite
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], [[def-linear-map]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); its entry
$G_{ij}$ has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}\gamma_{j}^{-1}$ and the
quadratic quantity $\frac12v^{\mathsf T}G(q)v$ has dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ for every choice of coordinate dimensions.
$\widetilde L$ is of class $C^{2}$; the **substituted action** of an admissible
coordinate curve $q:[a,b]\to\Omega$ with $[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$ is
$\widetilde S(q):=\int_{a}^{b}\widetilde L(t,q(t),q'(t))dt$ whenever the
chart conventions of [[def-cm07-action-and-mechanical-lagrangian]] apply to
$\widetilde L$, and the **Lagrange operator** of $\widetilde L$ is

$$\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t):=\frac{d}{dt}\Bigl(\frac{\partial\widetilde L}{\partial v}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\Bigr)-\frac{\partial\widetilde L}{\partial q}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{r}.$$

**(c) Generalized forces.** Let $f:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$
be a force field of the model's standing regularity
([[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii)) — for instance the residual
force $d$ of the presentation, or the model's full force map $F$. Its
**generalized force** in the coordinates $X$ is

$$Q_{f}(t,q,v):=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}f\bigl(t,X(q),DX(q)v\bigr)\in\mathbb R^{r};$$

its $i$-th component has the dimension of energy per unit of the coordinate
$q_{i}$, namely $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}\gamma_{i}^{-1}$: the Jacobian factor
$\partial X_{a}/\partial q_{i}$ carries the dimension $\ell\gamma_{i}^{-1}$ and
the force $f_{a}$ the dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$. Thus $Q_{f}\cdot\delta q$
has energy dimension; for a length-valued coordinate $Q_{f,i}$ has force
dimension, and for a dimensionless angle it has torque dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$. For the presentation
$(U,d)$ write $Q^{\mathrm{res}}:=Q_{d}$ for the generalized force of the
residual part; when $d\equiv0$ one has $Q^{\mathrm{res}}\equiv0$.

**(d) Constraint parametrizations.** Let a regular holonomic-constraint datum
$(O,k,g_{c})$ of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]] be given, where
$g_{c}:=G$ is the constraint map called $G$ in that definition; this separate
notation distinguishes it from the kinetic matrix $G(q)$ in clause (b). Let
$\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be its time-independent configuration
locus, so $\Sigma=\{(t,x)\in O:x\in\mathcal C\}$ (the scleronomic case).
A **parametrization of the constrained configurations** is a
generalized-coordinate map $X:\Omega\to Q$ with $r=3N-k$,
$X(\Omega)=\mathcal C\cap Q$, and $(t,X(q))\in O$ for all
$(t,q)\in I_{0}\times\Omega$. Thus $X$ covers every constrained configuration,
but a configuration may have more than one coordinate representative; a
covering or other surjective immersion is allowed. Injectivity is an optional
additional condition for applications that require unique coordinates. Each
admissible coordinate curve induces a constrained curve family with permitted
velocity; the reduction theorem of this page also identifies the virtual
displacements with the image of $DX$.

**(e) Declared Lagrange equations.** With the data of clauses (a)-(c), the
model with presentation $(U,d)$ **declares as its Lagrange equations in the
coordinates $X$**

$$\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in J),$$

posed for $C^{2}$ admissible coordinate curves $q:J\to\Omega$. These equations
are part of the coordinate description: for $d\equiv0$ they reduce to the
Euler-Lagrange equation $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)=0$ of the substituted
Lagrangian. For a chart ($r=3N$), the transport identity of
[[prop-cm-coordinate-covariance-of-the-euler-lagrange-expression]] clause 4,
applied to the time-independent map $X$, gives
$\Lambda(\widetilde L)=DX^{\mathsf T}(\mathsf Mx''-F+d)$ along
$x=X\circ q$: here $L_v=\mathsf Mx'$ and $L_x=-\nabla_xU$, while
$F=-\nabla_xU+d$. Hence $\Lambda(\widetilde L)=DX^{\mathsf T}d$
is equivalent to $\mathsf Mx''=F$, since $DX^{\mathsf T}$ is invertible.
On any interval $J$, the transport calculation applies on compact
subintervals around each interior time and extends to included endpoints
by continuity of these expressions. Whether
the same equations describe an ideal constrained motion for a
parametrization of clause (d) is a separate statement, proved as the reduction
theorem of this page; it is not part of this definition.

**(f) Status.** This item defines the dictionary between the Cartesian and the
generalized-coordinate descriptions: the coordinate map, the substituted
Lagrangian, the kinetic metric, generalized forces and the declared Lagrange
equations. It adopts no force law beyond the model's presentation, asserts no
solution existence and makes no empirical claim; the equivalence of the
declared equations with the model's Cartesian equation (for charts) and with
the ideal constrained equation (for parametrizations) is proved on this page.

Adopt the force-branch data of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N_{p}\ge1$
labelled particles with masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N_{p}}>0$, an open time window
$I_{0}$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N_{p}}$ and a force map
$F$ with the standing regularity; adopt a regular holonomic-constraint datum
$(O,k,g_{c})$ of [[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]], where $g_{c}:=G$
is the constraint map named $G$ in that definition, and the ideal-reaction law
of [[post-cm06-ideal-reaction-law]]. Assume the datum is **scleronomic with
time-independent locus** $\mathcal C\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N_{p}}$:

$$\Sigma=\bigl\{(t,x)\in O:\ x\in\mathcal C\bigr\}.$$

Let $(U,d)$ be a potential presentation of $F$ in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]], so that
$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v)$. Let $r:=3N_{p}-k$,
let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^{r}$ be open and nonempty, and let
$X:\Omega\to Q$ be a **parametrization of the constrained configurations** in
the sense of clause (d) of [[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]]:
$X$ is of class $C^{3}$, $DX(q)$ is injective for every $q\in\Omega$,
$X(\Omega)=\mathcal C\cap Q$ and $(t,X(q))\in O$ for all
$(t,q)\in I_{0}\times\Omega$. Injectivity of $X$ is not assumed: the image
condition requires coverage of the constrained configurations, while multiple
coordinate representatives are permitted. Define the kinetic matrix,
substituted potential, substituted Lagrangian and
residual generalized force

$$\mathsf G(q):=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}\mathsf M\,DX(q),\qquad \widetilde U(t,q):=U\bigl(t,X(q)\bigr),\qquad \widetilde L(t,q,v):=\tfrac12\,v^{\mathsf T}\mathsf G(q)v-\widetilde U(t,q),$$

$$Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q,v):=DX(q)^{\mathsf T}d\bigl(t,X(q),DX(q)v\bigr).$$

Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with nonempty interior, let $q:J\to\Omega$
be a $C^{2}$ curve and put $x:=X\circ q$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $x$ is a constrained motion of the model with an ideal reaction field: there
   is a continuous $R:J\to\mathbb R^{3N_{p}}$ with
   $\mathsf M x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)+R(t)$ and
   $R(t)\cdot\delta=0$ for every $t\in J$ and every virtual displacement
   $\delta\in\ker D_{x}g_{c}(t,x(t))$;
2. $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)(t)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)$ for
   every $t\in J$, i.e. the declared Lagrange equations of
   [[def-cm07-generalized-coordinates-and-forces]] hold along $q$.

If these hold, then:

3. the reaction is unique: $R(t)=\mathsf M x''(t)-F(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every
   $t\in J$, and there is a unique continuous
   $\lambda:J\to\mathbb R^{k}$ with
   $R(t)=D_{x}g_{c}(t,x(t))^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t)$;
   if the declared constraint components have dimensions $\gamma_{\alpha}$,
   then $[\lambda_{\alpha}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}/\gamma_{\alpha}$;
4. the virtual displacements at $x(t)$ are exactly the image of $DX(q(t))$,
   $\ker D_{x}g_{c}(t,x(t))=DX(q(t))\bigl(\mathbb R^{r}\bigr)$;
5. the statement is conditional on the adopted force branch, the presentation,
   the scleronomic regular constraint datum and the ideal-reaction law. No
   solution existence, no uniqueness of the coordinate curve for given data
   and no empirical content are asserted.

Adopt the force branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$ particle
labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$, a nondegenerate open time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), identify
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}=\mathbb R^{3N}$ with the position
tuple of the labels ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and let $\mathsf M$ be the
mass operator of clause (d) of that definition, $\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})
=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N})$, a symmetric positive definite linear map with
block-diagonal matrix and blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$. All components below are read in
this frame, and dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]].

**(a) Constraint datum.** A **holonomic-constraint datum** on this data is a
triple $(O,k,G)$ with:

1. an **ambient set** $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, open and
   nonempty;
2. an integer $k$ with $1\le k\le 3N-1$;
3. a map $G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\to\mathbb R^{k}$ of class $C^{2}$
   ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), each component carrying a
   declared dimension $[G_{\alpha}]=\gamma_{\alpha}$ fixed by the model (the
   model may rescale a component by a nonzero constant, which changes
   $\gamma_{\alpha}$ and the component but not its zero set);

subject to the two hypotheses

4. **nonempty admissible locus:** the **constraint locus**
   $$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x)\in O:\ G(t,x)=0\bigr\}$$
   is nonempty and contained in $I_{0}\times Q$: every constrained
   configuration is an admissible configuration of the force-branch model and
   every constrained time lies in its time window;
5. **regularity:** for every $(t,x)\in\Sigma$ the Jacobian $D_{x}G(t,x)$
   ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]) is surjective, equivalently has rank
   $k$.

For $t\in\mathbb R$ write $\Sigma_{t}:=\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:(t,x)\in\Sigma\}$
for the **instantaneous constraint locus**. Here a **$C^{2}$ embedded
submanifold of dimension $d$** in $\mathbb R^{n}$ means a subset $S$, with
its inherited topology, such that each $p\in S$ has an open neighbourhood
$U\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}$ and a $C^{2}$ diffeomorphism
$h:U\to W$ onto an open $W\subseteq\mathbb R^{n}$ satisfying
$h(S\cap U)=W\cap(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{0\})$; both $h$ and its inverse
are $C^{2}$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
This is the finite-regularity slice convention used for these loci;
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]] instead requires smooth charts.

Each nonempty $\Sigma_t$ is a $C^{2}$ embedded submanifold of dimension
$3N-k$. Indeed, at any $p\in\Sigma_t$ choose $k$ spatial columns of
$D_xG(t,p)$ giving an invertible minor, and permute coordinates as
$x=(u,v)\in\mathbb R^{3N-k}\times\mathbb R^k$. The fixed-time map
$H(u,v):=G(t,(u,v))$ is $C^2$ on the open slice of $O$, vanishes at $p$,
and has invertible $D_vH(p)$. Apply
[[thm-parametrized-implicit-function-theorem-with-higher-regularity]] with
regularity order $2$ and no parameter block: on open neighbourhoods
$P\times Q$ of $p$, its zero set is exactly $v=\varphi(u)$ for a
$C^2$ map $\varphi:P\to Q$. The map
$h(u,v)=(u,v-\varphi(u))$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism onto the open set
$W=\{(u,w):u\in P,\ w+\varphi(u)\in Q\}$, with inverse
$(u,w)\mapsto(u,w+\varphi(u))$, and sends that graph to
$W\cap(\mathbb R^{3N-k}\times\{0\})$. This proves the claimed local
slice property. If $G$ is smooth, the smooth regular-value terminology of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]] and the smooth conclusion of
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] also apply.
When $k=3N-1$ the instantaneous locus is locally a $C^2$ curve, and the number
$$\dim\Sigma_{t}=3N-k$$
is the **instantaneous degrees of freedom** of the constrained branch. The
set $V(t,x):=\ker D_{x}G(t,x)\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ has dimension $3N-k$ by
the rank-nullity theorem for matrices ([[cor-matrix-rank-nullity]]) and is called the space of **virtual displacements** of the datum
at $(t,x)$; its elements are the first-order differences of constrained
configurations at fixed time, in the sense of the mathematical definition
[[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]. A vector
$v\in\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a **permitted velocity** at $(t,x)\in O$ when
$$G_{t}(t,x)+D_{x}G(t,x)\,v=0 .$$

**(b) Constrained curve families.** Let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an interval with
nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). A **constrained curve family** of the
datum is a map $x:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ of class $C^{2}$ with
$(t,x(t))\in O$ and $G(t,x(t))=0$ for every $t\in J$; writing
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with coordinate curves $x_{i}:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ and
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$, the componentwise derivatives of
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]];
$w_{i}$ is the coordinate velocity of label $i$), the chain rule
([[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]) applied to $t\mapsto G(t,x(t))$
gives
$$G_{t}\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)+D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)\,w(t)=0\qquad(t\in J),$$
so the velocity of a $C^{1}$ constrained curve family is permitted at every
time. A tuple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})\in O\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ is **consistent
data** of the datum when $G(t_{0},x_{0})=0$ and
$G_{t}(t_{0},x_{0})+D_{x}G(t_{0},x_{0})v_{0}=0$; these are the initial data at
which constrained motions are posed below.

**(c) Reaction field and the constrained equation.** A **reaction field along
a curve family** $x:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ is a continuous map
$R:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, of force dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$ in each
component. The **equation of the constrained datum along $x$** is
$$\mathsf M\,x''(t)=F\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)+R(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
componentwise $m_{i}x_{i}''(t)=F_{i}(t,x(t),w(t))+R_{i}(t)$. A
**holonomic-constraint model** consists of the force-branch data, a
holonomic-constraint datum $(O,k,G)$, and the declaration that the position
tuple of the labels satisfies $G(t,x(t))=0$ for all times while a reaction
field acts: a **constrained motion** of the model (with reaction $R$) is a
constrained curve family $x:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ together with a reaction field
$R$ satisfying the displayed equation. The force map $F$ is the model's
declared interaction force of the force branch, and $R$ is the additional
force contribution exerted by the mechanism that realizes the constraint; the
total force along a constrained motion is the pointwise sum $F+R$ in the sense
of clause (v) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]], read along the curve. The
reaction is **not** part of the force map: the constrained branch is the branch
excluded by clause (i) of that postulate, and the equation above is the
adopted equation of the constrained model. For any specified constrained curve
family $x$, this equation fixes the reaction uniquely as the residual field
$$R(t)=\mathsf Mx''(t)-F\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr).$$
Without an additional reaction law, the constraint and this equation do not
select which constrained curve families are dynamically admissible: every
$C^{2}$ constrained curve can be paired with its continuous residual field to
satisfy the equation. The ideal-reaction law of the postulate of this page is
the additional model assumption that selects among these candidates by
requiring the reaction to annihilate the virtual displacements.

**(d) Scleronomic and rheonomic constraints.** The datum is **scleronomic**
when the constraint locus is time-independent, in the precise sense that there
is a set $N\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with
$$\Sigma=\bigl\{(t,x)\in O:\ x\in N\bigr\};$$
equivalently, membership in the locus is a condition on $x$ alone within $O$:
if $(t,x)\in\Sigma$ and $(t',x)\in O$, then $(t',x)\in\Sigma$ (the two
formulations are exchanged by passing between $N$ and the projection of
$\Sigma$ to $\mathbb R^{3N}$). For the standard product ambient set
$O=I_{0}\times Q$ the condition reads $\Sigma=I_{0}\times(N\cap Q)$. The datum
is **rheonomic** otherwise.

If the datum is scleronomic, then the declared presentation $G$, and every
$C^{2}$ presentation of the same locus with the rank hypothesis, satisfy
$$G_{t}(t,x)=0\qquad\text{for every }(t,x)\in\Sigma,$$
because for $x\in N$ every $(t,x)\in O$ lies in $\Sigma$, so $t\mapsto G(t,x)$
vanishes identically on the open set of times $\{t:(t,x)\in O\}$; this is the
form in which the classification is used by the balance theorems of this page.

The identity is a consequence of time-independence and **not** a criterion for
it. Write $s(x):=(x_{1})_{1}\in\mathbb R$ for the first Cartesian
component of particle $1$, of length dimension $\ell$, and fix a nonzero
speed $u$ of dimension $\ell\tau^{-1}$. The scalar presentation
$G(t,x):=(s(x)-ut)^{2}$, of dimension $\ell^{2}$, on
$O=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ has the moving zero set $\{s(x)=ut\}$ while
$G_{t}(t,x)=-2u(s(x)-ut)$ vanishes at every point of that set; this presentation
violates the rank hypothesis, but the identity can also hold for a
rank-regular presentation: on
$O=\bigl((0,T_{*})\cup(2T_{*},3T_{*})\bigr)\times\mathbb R^{3N}$,
with $T_{*}>0$ of time dimension, the scalar $C^{2}$ map equal to
$s(x)$ on $(0,T_{*})\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ and to a fixed
$L_{*}>0$ of length dimension on $(2T_{*},3T_{*})\times\mathbb R^{3N}$
has dimension $\ell$ and the rank-$1$ zero set
$\Sigma=(0,T_{*})\times\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:s(x)=0\}$ with $G_{t}=0$ on $\Sigma$,
yet $\Sigma$ is not of the form $\{(t,x)\in O:x\in N\}$ for any $N$: the point
$(T_{*}/2,0)\in\Sigma$ would force $0\in N$, and then $(5T_{*}/2,0)\in O$ would lie in
$\Sigma$. Hence the classification is a property of the locus, and the
identity is used only in the direction proved above.

Under a nowhere-vanishing $C^{2}$ rescaling $G'=\rho G$ one has
$D_{x}G'=\rho\,D_{x}G$ and $G'_{t}=\rho_{t}G+\rho G_{t}=\rho G_{t}$ at the
points of $\Sigma$, so the virtual displacements and permitted velocities are
unchanged, the multiplier of a motion transforms as
$\lambda'=\rho^{-1}\lambda$, and the reaction $D_{x}G'^{\mathsf T}\lambda'$
and the product $-\lambda'\cdot G'_{t}=-\lambda\cdot G_{t}$ of the rheonomic
power theorem are unchanged at the locus.

**(e) Status.** This item defines a model class: it fixes the constraint
datum, the constrained curves, the virtual displacements, the reaction field
and the equation of the constrained branch. It adopts no ideal-reaction law
(that is the content of the ideal-reaction postulate of this page), no particular force
law, and no measured value. Whether a concrete apparatus — a frictionless
joint, a smooth track, a taut rod or string, a no-slip contact — is described
by a holonomic-constraint model is an application-level judgement recorded with
the apparatus, together with the regime in which the rigidity, frictionlessness
or contact assumptions are adequate; the framework itself attaches no empirical
claim to the class.

Adopt as a physical assumption of the framework, in the setting of
[[def-cm06-holonomic-constraint-model]]:

**(i) The ideal-reaction law.** Along every constrained motion $x:J\to
\mathbb R^{3N}$ of a holonomic-constraint model, with reaction field
$R:J\to\mathbb R^{3N}$, the reaction annihilates every virtual displacement:

$$R(t)\cdot\delta=0\qquad\text{for every }t\in J\text{ and every }\delta\in V\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)=\ker D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),$$

the pairing being the Euclidean inner product of $\mathbb R^{3N}$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). This is the **d'Alembert condition** (the
condition of zero virtual work of the reaction) in the sense of
[[def-cm-holonomic-constraint-and-ideal-reactions]]. By the multiplier lemma
[[lem-cm-constraint-multipliers-and-accelerations]], applied at each time with
the surjective Jacobian $D_{x}G(t,x(t))$, the condition holds at time $t$ if
and only if there is a unique $\lambda(t)\in\mathbb R^{k}$ with
$$R(t)=D_{x}G\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr)^{\mathsf T}\lambda(t);$$
this representation is a mathematical consequence of the condition and the
rank hypothesis, not a separate assumption, and the multiplier has dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}/\gamma_{\alpha}$ in component $\alpha$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The condition is imposed only along the motions of the
model, and it does not by itself determine $R$: it constrains $R$ at each time
to the $k$-dimensional conormal space, and which element occurs is fixed by
the twice-differentiated constraint through the balance theorem of this page.

**(ii) What is adopted.** Clause (i) is an adopted restriction on the
mechanism that realizes the constraint, not a theorem about bodies, tracks or
contacts. It is the idealization of a mechanism that exerts only the reaction
needed to maintain the constraint, distributed normally to the admissible
directions at each instant; the force branch of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] excludes constraint reactions from its force
maps, and this postulate is the additional law that closes the constrained
branch.

**(iii) Intended model identifications.** The framework intends clause (i) to
model, subject to the qualifications of clause (iv): frictionless hinges and
joints; smooth bilateral contacts and tracks; a taut light rod, and a taut
string while it stays taut; and no-slip rolling in the planar holonomic case,
provided the contact can supply the required tangential reaction. Each of
these identifications is an application-level statement made and recorded with
the apparatus; the framework asserts no measurement, no material parameter and
no numerical value here.

**(iv) Limits of the idealization.** The law is **not** asserted for:

1. constraints with dry sliding friction along an admissible direction, whose
   force has a component doing virtual work on admissible displacements — such
   friction must be declared as a separate force contribution with its own
   model;
2. unilateral contacts and mechanisms that can release the constraint (a bead
   on the outside of a surface, a string that can go slack, a block that can
   separate), which are maintained only while the required reaction satisfies
   a one-sided capability condition; where the condition fails, the constraint
   is released and a contact-change model is required, and none is supplied
   here;
3. points where the Jacobian $D_{x}G$ drops rank, which lie outside the
   regularity hypothesis of the datum and outside the representation above;
4. direct active forces on the modelled labels with a component along an
   admissible virtual displacement: these must be declared as additional
   force contributions. Prescribed motion of a support is instead encoded
   in the time-dependent constraint $G$ and is compatible with clause (i);
   its ideal reaction may do actual work as in clause (v). The dynamics and
   energy budget of equipment driving that support are not modelled here;
5. any claim that the mechanism can mechanically supply the computed
   reaction: the law computes the reaction the ideal constraint exerts; whether
   a physical contact, rod or string can supply it (friction cone, sign of a
   tensile force, strength limits, no-slip conditions) is an additional
   premise of an application.

**(v) The law is not a work statement.** Clause (i) concerns virtual
displacements at fixed time; it does not assert that the reaction performs no
work along the motion. For a scleronomic constraint the reaction power
vanishes identically, but for a rheonomic constraint the reaction can do work,
with $R\cdot x'=-\lambda\cdot G_{t}$; the precise statement, its static case
and worked models are the content of the rheonomic-power theorem and the
companion examples of this page.

**(vi) Status and empirical content.** The clause is adopted, not deduced; the
sources record the ideal-reaction condition as an additional physical
hypothesis attached to a constraint, not as a consequence of writing the
constraint down. The passage from clause (i) to the constrained equation of
motion is a theorem with explicit regularity hypotheses, proved on this page.
Whether the idealization is adequate for a given apparatus is decided by
comparing the model's conditional predictions with reported observations under
the stated regime, with the qualifications of clause (iv) carried along;
agreement of such a comparison is evidence about the combined model and
apparatus, not a proof of the idealization.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, the **transpose** of $A$ is the matrix
$A^{\mathsf T}\in M_{n\times m}(F)$ defined by

$$(A^{\mathsf T})_{ji}:=a_{ij}.$$

Thus transposition interchanges rows and columns. The transpose of a zero-sized
matrix is the unique matrix of the transposed zero-sized shape.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

derivations.claim: By [F5] the presentation is hyperregular on the Cartesian chart with $H(t,x,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot\mathsf M^{-1}p+U(t,x)$, so $H_{p}(t,x,p)=\mathsf M^{-1}p$ and $H_{x}(t,x,p)=\nabla_{x}U(t,x)$; by [F5] the momentum curve $p=\mathsf Mx'$ is the fibre derivative $\mathcal L_{v}(t,x,x')$ along $x$, so the branch hypothesis of [F4] is met on every state of the curve.

Clause 3: by [F6] the substituted Lagrangian is the mechanical chart Lagrangian $\widetilde L=\tfrac12v^{\mathsf T}G(q)v-\widetilde U(t,q)$ with $G$ symmetric positive definite and $\widetilde L_{v}(t,q,v)=G(q)v$, and by [F5] its chart is hyperregular with $p=\widetilde L_{v}(t,q,q')=G(q)q'$, $\widetilde H(t,q,p)=\tfrac12p\cdot G(q)^{-1}p+\widetilde U(t,q)$ and $\widetilde H_{p}=G(q)^{-1}p$, $\widetilde H_{q}=-\widetilde L_{q}(t,q,G(q)^{-1}p)$ by [F4]; explicitly its $i$-th component is $\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}(\partial_{q_i}G(q)^{-1})p+\partial_{q_i}\widetilde U(t,q)$, retaining the kinetic contribution when $G$ varies, with derivatives computed using [F8]; the Lagrange operator is $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)=\frac{d}{dt}\widetilde L_{v}(t,q,q')-\widetilde L_{q}(t,q,q')=-E_{\widetilde L}(q)$, so by [F4] applied to $\widetilde L$ the equation $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)=0$ is equivalent to $q'=\widetilde H_{p}$ and $p'=-\widetilde H_{q}$.

Clause 1, (a)$\Leftrightarrow$(b): by [F3] the motions of the model on the global potential branch are exactly, through their restrictions to closed subintervals, the stationary curves of the action, and by [F2] the motion condition of clause 1(a) is $\mathsf Mx''=-\nabla_{x}U$ on $J$, equivalently $E_{L}(x)(t)=0$ for all $t\in J$; by [F4] the pair $(x,p)$ satisfies Hamilton's equations if and only if $x$ is $C^{2}$ with $E_{L}(x)=0$ and $p=\mathcal L_{v}(t,x,x')$, which by step 1.1 is exactly $p=\mathsf Mx'$; hence clause 1(a) is equivalent to clause 1(b).

Clause 2: with $p=\mathsf Mx'$ one has $p'=\mathsf Mx''$, $H_{p}=\mathsf M^{-1}p=x'$ and $H_{x}=\nabla_{x}U$ by step 1.1, all computed with [F8]; hence $\mathsf Mx''=-\nabla_{x}U+d(t,x,x')$ holds exactly when $x'=H_{p}$ and $p'=-H_{x}+d(t,x,\mathsf M^{-1}p)$, since the first identity is equivalent to $x'=\mathsf M^{-1}p$ and the second is the displayed equation with $x'$ replaced by $\mathsf M^{-1}p$.

Clause 3 with residual force: adding $Q^{\mathrm{res}}$ to both sides of the Lagrange equation adds the same term to the momentum equation, because by [F4] the momentum is $p=\widetilde L_{v}(t,q,q')$ and $\widetilde H_{q}=-\widetilde L_{q}$ on the branch; hence $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q,q')$ is equivalent to $p'=-\widetilde H_{q}+Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q,q')$ together with $q'=\widetilde H_{p}$, in both directions.

Clause 1, (c)$\Leftrightarrow$(b): by [F2] the restriction $x|_{[a,b]}$ is stationary for the action of $L$ on $[a,b]$ if and only if $E_{L}(x)$ vanishes on $[a,b]$; $J$ is the union of its closed subintervals, so clause 1(c) holds exactly when $E_{L}(x)$ vanishes on $J$, which by step 2.1 is equivalent to clause 1(b).

Clause 4: under the stated hypotheses [F7] identifies the constrained-motion condition with the declared Lagrange equation $\Lambda(\widetilde L)(q)=Q^{\mathrm{res}}(t,q,q')$, and $Q^{\mathrm{res}}\equiv0$ because $d\equiv0$; by step 2.3 this is equivalent to the Hamilton system of clause 3.
Collecting: clause 1 follows from steps 2.1 and 3.1, clause 2 from step 2.2, clause 3 from steps 1.2 and 2.3, and clause 4 from step 3.2.

boundaries.reason: Statement fixes a curve on an interval with nonempty interior and a chart with positive-size velocity slots; steps 2.1 and 3.1 use actual closed subintervals of that interval.

boundaries.evidence: Zero momentum and zero velocity states are included: the equivalences of steps 2.2, 2.3 and 3.1 are stated for every $t$ in the interval, including states with $p(t)=0$ or $x'(t)=0$.
The one-label and one-coordinate cases are included; the statements are general in $N$ and in the dimension $r$ of the coordinate chart.
The singular velocity Hessian is excluded by the hyperregularity of the mechanical branch used in steps 1.1 and 1.2; no degenerate presentation enters the equivalences.

The interval $J$ is open and stationarity is read on every closed subinterval $[a,b]\subseteq J$ with the fixed-endpoint convention of the cited chart definition; steps 2.1 and 3.1 treat both the interior equivalence and the closed-subinterval reading.

boundaries.reason: The phase curve is explicitly p=mass*x-prime or P=G*q-prime; step 2.3 algebraically inserts the given residual force, and no family of solution curves is selected.

boundaries.evidence: The forward directions are established: step 2.1 (motion implies Hamilton), step 3.1 (stationarity implies Hamilton), step 1.2 (declared Lagrange equations imply the Hamilton system) and step 3.2 (constrained motion implies the Lagrange equation).

The reverse directions are established: step 2.1 (Hamilton implies motion, via the Euler-Lagrange equivalence), step 3.1 (Hamilton implies stationarity), step 2.3 (the forced Hamilton system implies the Lagrange equation) and step 3.2 (the Lagrange equation implies the constrained motion).

risk_review.notes: Eight proof steps checked in both directions. With p=Mx prime, the first equation is automatic and momentum equation is Newton with residual force retained. Generalized H_q includes derivative of G inverse. Stationarity on every closed subinterval is equivalent to EL on the open interval. Constraint reduction is used only for the stated scleronomic regular locus, C3 immersion and adopted ideal reaction; no coordinate lift uniqueness or solution existence inferred.

citations.quote:
Adopt one force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$ particle labels
with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ (clause (i)), an open nondegenerate time
window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$
and a force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ and identify position tuples with points of
$\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]); dimensions are
read by [[def-cm01-units]], inner products and norms are Euclidean
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]), and differentiability classes are those of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. Let $\mathsf M$ be the mass
operator of clause (d) of [[def-cm01-configuration]],
$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N})$, a symmetric
positive definite linear map of $\mathbb R^{3N}$.

**(a) Kinetic energy.** The **kinetic energy** of the labels at coordinate
velocity $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}=\mathbb R^{3N}$ is

$$K(v):=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{N}m_{i}\,\lvert v_{i}\rvert_{2}^{2}=\frac12\,v\cdot\mathsf M v .$$

$K$ is the restriction of a $C^{\infty}$ function of $(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and has
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (energy). Its Euclidean gradient is
$K'(v)=\mathsf M v$, because $\partial K/\partial v_{i}=m_{i}v_{i}$
([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]], [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]).

**(b) Mechanical Lagrangian of a potential presentation.** Let $(U,d)$ be a
potential presentation of the model's force map in the sense of clause (a) of
[[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]]: a function
$U:I_{0}\times Q\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^{2}$ with dimension
$\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ and residual forces $d=(d_{1},\dots,d_{N})$ such that
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v)$$
on the state domain. The **mechanical Lagrangian of the presentation** is

$$L:I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}\longrightarrow\mathbb R,\qquad L(t,x,v):=K(v)-U(t,x).$$

$L$ is of class $C^{2}$ on its open domain and has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
When $d\equiv0$ the presentation is a global potential model and $L$ is a
Lagrangian of the model itself; when $d\not\equiv0$, $L$ carries the potential
part only, and the residual force contribution $d$ is not included in $L$.
The
potential representative is part of the declared data: replacing $U$ by
$U+c(t)$ for differentiable $c:I_{0}\to\mathbb R$ replaces $L$ by $L-c(t)$
([[def-cm03-potential-and-mechanical-energy]] clause (c)).

**(c) Action, variations, stationarity.** Let $a<b$ be reals with
$[a,b]\subseteq I_{0}$. If $Q=\varnothing$, there is no map
$x:[a,b]\to Q$, so this clause has no action, variation or stationarity
instance. Assume $Q\ne\varnothing$ for the chart construction below, and put
$O:=I_{0}\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$. The set $O$ is open and contains
$[a,b]\times Q\times\mathbb R^{3N}$, so with $n:=3N$ the pair $(O,L)$ is a
time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times Q$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]. **Admissible
curves** (the $C^{2}$ curves $x:[a,b]\to Q$ with the extension convention of
that definition), **variations** $\eta$ with $\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0$, the
**action**

$$S(x):=\int_{a}^{b}L\bigl(t,x(t),x'(t)\bigr)\,dt,$$

the **first variation** $\delta S(x)[\eta]$ and **stationarity** of $x$ are the
notions of [[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] instantiated at this
chart; the derivative $x'$ is the coordinate velocity ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).
The action has dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (energy multiplied by time).
Write $E_{L}(x):[a,b]\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ for the Euler-Lagrange expression of
the instantiated chart.

**(d) Status.** This item defines the action functional and the Lagrangian of a
presentation from data already adopted in the model: no new force law, no
equation of motion and no measured value are introduced. The first variation
of $S$ exists for every admissible curve and variation and its formula, the
equivalence of stationarity with the vanishing of $E_{L}(x)$, and the relation
of both to the model's equation of motion are theorems of this page, not part
of the definition.

Adopt the force model and one inertial frame of
[[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]], with configuration domain $Q$, time
window $I_{0}$ and force map $F$. Dimensions are read by [[def-cm01-units]]
and gradients are Euclidean ([[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]); points of
$Q$ are written $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$ with $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$.

**(a) Potential representation of the force map.** A model **presents its
force map through a potential** when it declares a function
$$U:I_{0}\times Q\longrightarrow\mathbb R$$
of class $C^{2}$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), of
dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules), with
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N)$$
for every $(t,x,v)$ of the state domain; here $\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is the
gradient of $u\mapsto U(t,x_{1},\dots,x_{i-1},u,x_{i+1},\dots,x_{N})$ at
$u=x_{i}$. More generally, a model may declare **residual forces**
$d_{i}:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of the standing
regularity of clause (iii) of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and present
$$F_{i}(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U(t,x)+d_{i}(t,x,v);$$
the pair $(U,d)$ is then the model's presentation and
$F_{i}^{\mathrm{p}}:=-\nabla_{x_{i}}U$ is its **potential part**. The scalar
$U$ is a **potential energy** for the model's potential part; the framework's
earlier admission of potentials in [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (iii) is
the special case $d\equiv0$. A model that presents its whole force map this
way with $d\equiv0$ is a **global potential model** (the term "conservative
model" is used only in this sense).

**(b) Potential and mechanical energy along a curve family.** For a curve
family $x:J\to Q$ of the model ([[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]
clause (a)) define the **potential energy along the family** and the
**mechanical energy** by
$$U_{x}(t):=U\bigl(t,x(t)\bigr),\qquad E(t):=K(t)+U_{x}(t)\qquad(t\in J),$$
with $K$ the kinetic energy of the definition. The potential part contributes
to the force field but not directly to $K$; $E$ is defined only along the
potential branch of the model, and along a motion it is the subject of the
energy balance of this page.

**(c) Normalization of the potential.** Let $c:I_0\to\mathbb R$ be
differentiable and put $\widetilde U:=U+c(t)$, retaining $C^2$ regularity
when a potential presentation of the standing class is required. The spatial
gradient is unchanged, so this presents the same potential part with the same
residual forces. The full converse is componentwise: if $\widetilde U$ and
$U$ are $C^2$ and have the same spatial gradient, then on each connected
component $C$ of the open set $Q$ there is a $C^2$ function
$c_C:I_0\to\mathbb R$ with
$$\widetilde U(t,x)-U(t,x)=c_C(t)\qquad(x\in C).$$
Here a connected component is a maximal connected subset of $Q$. For fixed
$t$, the difference is constant on every ball contained in $Q$: along any
segment in the ball its derivative is the vanishing spatial gradient paired
with the segment direction. The difference is consequently locally constant,
and on a connected component it is constant, since a value's level set and
its complement are both relatively open. Evaluating at any fixed point of
$C$ gives the $C^2$ regularity of $c_C$. Conversely, independent such functions
on the components give a $C^2$ potential with unchanged spatial gradient;
components of an open Euclidean set are open, because each sufficiently small
ball about one of their points is connected and lies in that component.
A single $c(t)$ describes every ambiguity precisely when the component
functions agree, in particular when $Q$ is connected. No agreement follows
from openness alone: on two disjoint balls the potentials $0$ and the function
equal to $0$ on one ball and $1$ on the other have the same force. Every
continuous motion on an interval remains in one component, so its energy
shifts by that component's $c_C(t)$ and its energy rate by $c_C'(t)$.
The representative is part of the model's declaration, and every energy
statement names it.

**(d) Closed and exact force fields.** A **time- and velocity-independent
configuration-space force field** is a $C^{1}$ map
$\varphi=(\varphi_{1},\dots,\varphi_{N}):Q\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$, where
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is the open configuration domain and each
$\varphi_i(x)$ is the force on label $i$ at configuration $x$; its components
have force dimension. It represents a force map of the form
$F_i(t,x,v)=\varphi_i(x)$ on the model's state domain. This configuration-space
field is not in general an external single-label force: to identify its
$i$th component with an external map of [[post-cm02-interactions]] clause (i),
one must further require that it depend on $x_i$ alone, as in the declared
signature $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}(t,x_i,v_i)$. Such a field is **closed** when
$\partial_{k}\varphi_{j}=\partial_{j}\varphi_{k}$ for all coordinate indices
$j,k\in\{0,\dots,3N-1\}$ at every point of $Q$, using the flattened
coordinate indices of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]], and **exact with potential
energy $U$** when $\varphi=-\nabla U$ for a $C^{2}$ function
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$; equivalently, the field $-\varphi$ is exact in the sense
of [[def-closed-and-exact-c1-vector-fields]] with potential $U$. The following
mathematical facts are used, with their proofs at the cited items:

1. every exact field is closed, by equality of mixed partial derivatives
   ([[thm-clairaut-schwarz-mixed-partials]], applied to the $C^2$ potential);
2. on a star-shaped open domain every closed $C^{1}$ field is exact, by the
   Poincaré lemma ([[thm-poincare-lemma-for-star-shaped-domains]]);
3. beyond item 2 this item asserts **no** implication from closedness to
   global exactness: on a general open domain a closed field need not have a
   potential energy, and the criterion used by the framework is exactness as
   defined above.

Consequently the existence of a global potential energy on the model's
configuration domain is a property of the field on that domain, and a model
whose potential part is a merely closed field on a non-star-shaped domain is
not thereby a global potential model. The distinction is sharp: the
companion examples page carries a model on an annular domain whose force
field is smooth and closed, has nonzero circulation around a closed loop, and
therefore admits no global potential and no global conserved energy of the
form $K+U$, while item 2 provides a local potential and a locally conserved
energy on every star-shaped subpart of that domain.

**(e) Local potentials.** Let $V\subseteq Q$ be open and star-shaped with
respect to one of its points ([[def-star-shaped-open-subset-of-rn]]) and let
$\varphi$ be closed on $V$. Then item 2 of (d) provides a $C^{2}$ potential
$U_{V}:V\to\mathbb R$ with $\varphi|_{V}=-\nabla U_{V}$: a **local potential**
of the field on $V$. On the restricted configuration domain $V$ the model
with force $-\nabla U_{V}$ is a global potential model, so the mechanical
energy $K+U_{V}$ is available along curve families in $V$; this is how a
potential is recovered from a merely closed field on a sufficiently small
star-shaped piece of the domain, with no claim of a global representative.

**(f) Equipotential level sets.** For this clause assume additionally that
$U:Q\to\mathbb R$ is smooth, meaning $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); the potential presentations
of clause (a) still require only $C^2$. Let
$c\in\mathbb R$ and suppose $U^{-1}(c)\neq\varnothing$ and $\nabla
U(x)\neq0$ for every $x\in U^{-1}(c)$; equivalently $c$ is a regular value of
$U$ and every point of the level set is a regular point
([[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]]). Then $U^{-1}(c)$ is an
embedded submanifold of $Q$ of dimension $3N-1$
([[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]],
[[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]). No such conclusion is made at a
level where $\nabla U$ vanishes somewhere on the level set, where the level
set may have singular points.

**(g) Status.** The potential, its normalization, the residual forces and the
declaration of a potential presentation are model data; the closed/exact
statements of (d)-(f) are cited mathematics about the declared field. This
item asserts no conservation law, no force law of nature and no measured
value.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
